transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [name]. What brings you in to see me today?

I… I’m here because I keep hearing people talking about me. Like through the conference room walls, or sometimes from my phone even when it’s off. It sounds like board members or staff saying I’m ruining the company. It’s clear enough that I’ll answer before I realize… no one else heard it.
How long have you been hearing these voices—did this start recently, like in the past few days or weeks, or has it been going on for months?
It’s… not just the last few days. I think it’s been about three months now. The voices from the walls, or the phone… around then.
During these past three months, have you also been feeling unusually sad, hopeless, or low in energy—or alternatively, unusually elevated, irritable, or full of energy—for extended periods?
I don’t know… not really like that. I’ve been stressed and tired, but I wouldn’t say I’ve had some long stretch of being really depressed or, um, unusually energized.
Have you been using any drugs, alcohol, or other substances—recreational or prescribed—around the time these voices started, or in the past few months?
I… don’t really know. I mean, I don’t think anything changed around then. Nothing that stands out.
Since these experiences started about three months ago, have you noticed any changes in how you're able to function at work, socially, or in taking care of yourself day-to-day?

Yes… it has affected things. Work mostly. I’m not really keeping up with running the division like I used to, and some of the senior staff have… stepped in, I guess. They handle decisions I should be making.

At home, too. My husband’s been doing most of it because I either don’t finish things or I just… don’t start them.

Besides hearing these voices, have you noticed any changes in how you think or speak—like your thoughts feeling jumbled or hard to organize—or has anyone commented that your speech or behavior seems unusual to them?

I guess… yes. People have noticed I do odd things sometimes. In meetings, or at events, I’ll suddenly get up and move pens or name cards around into… patterns. Or I’ll repeat something someone just said without meaning to.

There have been times I’ve held my hands up like I’m presenting something, but it didn’t fit what was happening. Afterward I can tell it didn’t make sense. I just don’t really know why I did it.
Can you tell me specifically whether you have used alcohol, marijuana, stimulants, or any prescription or over-the-counter medications in the past few months, even occasionally?
I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I don’t think there’s been anything… notable. I haven’t been keeping track of every little thing.
Would you be open to having a urine drug screen done today to check for any substances that might be contributing to what you're experiencing?
I… I guess so. If you think it’s necessary. I don’t really see what it would show, but… yes, I can do it.
Does anyone in your family—parents, siblings, or other close relatives—have a history of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or other serious mental illness?
I’m not really sure. My family doesn’t talk much about that kind of thing. I don’t know of anyone, not… officially, anyway.

Has there been any period in the last three months—even just a few days—when you were completely off any alcohol, marijuana, or other substances, and if so, did you still hear the voices during that time?

Yes… there have been days like that. And I still heard them.

It’s mostly at work, like through the conference room walls, or sometimes from my phone even when it’s off. People talking about me… saying I’m ruining the company. It sounds real enough that I’ll answer before I realize no one else heard anything.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports persistent auditory hallucinations (voices commenting on her through walls/phone) for approximately 3 months, accompanied by disorganized/catatonic-like behaviors (arranging objects into patterns, echolalia, purposeless posturing) and clear functional decline at work and home. No sustained mood episode (depressive or manic) accompanies the psychosis, arguing against schizoaffective disorder or a mood disorder with psychotic features. Symptoms persisted during confirmed substance-free periods, and there is no clear temporal link to substance use, arguing against substance-induced psychosis. Duration exceeds 1 month of active symptoms with 3 months of continuous disturbance, meeting criteria for schizophrenia rather than brief psychotic disorder or schizophreniform disorder. Given the absence of a specified subtype and mixed symptom presentation (hallucinations, disorganized behavior, negative functional symptoms), unspecified schizophrenia is the most accurate code.
